metadata.title: Screens the Deal. Doesn't Decide It.
metadata.subtitle: The Deal-Screening Skill (Financial Services)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when you ask Claude to screen a deal, is it deciding whether the fund should pursue it, or running a fixed spec on what you give it? Lands the carry-out that deal-screening doesn't author the decision — it runs the SKILL.md's pass/fail checks on your inputs and hands you a memo, the same way every time.

beats.narration_text: People ask if deal-screening decides whether the fund should pursue a deal. It doesn't. Liam here, in for Bear — let's take the skill apart and see what it actually does with your inputs.

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually in a skill. It's a folder Claude reads before it works. Deal-screening's folder holds a SKILL.md — plain-language instructions, no hidden logic, no model weights doing something different behind the scenes. Claude reads that file, then acts on it. They optimized for one thing here: the file is the program. What you can see is what will run.

The instructions sit in a Steps section. Claude reads each step and runs it — top to bottom, one after another, no reordering, no shortcuts. It only branches when a step itself says to branch. That's the trade: reproducibility over cleverness. Same file, same steps, same behavior — every run.

production_viz.label: ONE STEP AT A TIME
production_viz.caption: no branching unless a step says so

beats.narration_text: Now, what the steps actually do. Three things, in order. Pull the deal's key metrics off whatever CIM or teaser you handed it. Push those metrics through a pass/fail check against your fund's stated investment criteria. Write a one-page screening memo. That's the whole job. Anything that isn't in the file's steps — arguing for the deal, guessing at fund fit, flagging red-flag counterparties — isn't part of what deal-screening does. They chose narrow-and-repeatable over broad-and-improvised.

Deal-screening doesn't author the decision. It runs the SKILL.md's pass/fail checks against the criteria you set, and hands you a memo — same procedure, same shape, every time. The judgment is still yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. Hand it a short deal — a regional trucking operator, revenue, EBITDA, net debt, asking price, why the seller is selling — plus a set of criteria your fund actually uses: sector, size band, valuation ceiling, concentration limits. Ask it to run the deal-screening skill on those inputs, and to walk you through the metric pulls, the pass/fail checks, and the one-page memo it would produce — but tell you what it's about to do before it does it. That last part is where you'll see the wiring instead of just the output. Go deeper: name one thing about the deal a pass/fail screen would miss, and describe the extra check your fund would need to bolt on to catch it.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to see how a deal-screening skill actually works. Here's a mini-CIM for a hypothetical target: 'Coastal Freight Co., a regional trucking operator; revenue $60M; EBITDA $9M; net debt $12M; asking price $75M enterprise value; owner selling for retirement, one-year transition offered; top customer ~18% of revenue.' My fund's investment criteria are: North American industrials, $5M–$15M EBITDA, EV/EBITDA under 8x, positive owner transition, no customer concentration over 25%. Walk me through, step by step, exactly what a deal-screening skill would do with these inputs — which metrics you would pull, which pass/fail checks you would run against my criteria, and what a one-page screening memo would look like as its output. Before you produce the memo, tell me what you're about to do so I can see the procedure, not just the result.
